html:
Bronze objects of astonishing detail found at Igbo-Ukwu, in southeastern Nigeria, and dated to about the 9th century CE. They are the oldest known bronze castings in West Africa.

In 1938 a man digging a water tank in his compound struck metal. The archaeologist Thurstan Shaw excavated the area around 1960. He found three sites: a store of ritual objects, a burial chamber of an important man seated with his regalia, and a pit of offerings.

The objects were made by lost wax casting. They include ritual vessels, bowls, a pot wrapped in cast rope, and a shell topped with an animal, covered in tiny beads, insects and fine lines. The metal came from local ores, so the work was African from start to finish. The tomb also held more than a hundred thousand glass and stone beads, some probably from far away, a sign of long distance trade.

The bronzes were made centuries before the Ife heads and the Benin Bronzes. They are often linked with the priest kings of the Igbo kingdom of Nri.
sum: Bronze objects of astonishing detail found at Igbo-Ukwu, in southeastern Nigeria, and dated to about the 9th century CE. They are the oldest known bronze castings in West Africa.
